bottom_line: In 804 men with chronic congestive heart failure receiving digoxin and diuretic therapy, enalapril vs hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate reduced mortality after two years (18 percent vs 25 percent; P = 0.016).
implications: These data support that, in this trial population, enalapril was associated with lower 2-year mortality than hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate (18 percent vs 25 percent; P = 0.016), with the difference attributed to fewer sudden deaths (e.g., sudden, no warning: 16% vs 25%). The document also reports no difference in pump-failure mortality (23% vs 19%; P = 0.44) and similar heart-failure hospitalization proportions (18.9 percent vs 18.4 percent), so the results do not establish superiority for those outcomes.

major_points.text: Double-blind randomized comparison in 804 men receiving digoxin and diuretics.
major_points.quote:
we compared the effects of hydralazine and isosorbide dinitrate with those of enala-
pril in 804 men receiving digoxin and diuretic therapy for
heart failure. The patients were randomly assigned in a
double-blind manner

major_points.text: Interventions were enalapril 20 mg daily vs hydralazine 300 mg plus isosorbide dinitrate 160 mg daily.
major_points.quote:
receive 20 mg of enalapril daily or
300 mg of hydralazine plus 160 mg of isosorbide dinitrate
daily.

major_points.text: Two-year mortality was significantly lower with enalapril than with hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate.
Overall mortality tended to be lower with enalapril but did not reach statistical significance.
major_points.quote:
and overall mortality
tended to be lower (P = 0.08).

major_points.text: Lower mortality with enalapril was attributed to a reduction in sudden death (with and without warning).
major_points.quote:
The lower mortality in the enalapril
arm was attributable to a reduction in the
incidence of sudden death

major_points.text: Hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate increased peak exercise oxygen consumption early; enalapril did not.
major_points.quote:
Oxygen consumption was
increased significantly by hydralazine—isosorbide di-
nitrate after 13 weeks (by 0.6 ml per kilogram per
minute; P<0.0001) and after 6 months (by 0.8 ml per
kilogram per minute; P<0.0001), but not by enalapril.

absolute_effects.text: Two-year mortality: enalapril 18 percent vs hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate 25 percent (P = 0.016).
Deaths during study: 132/403 (32.8 percent) with enalapril vs 153/401 (38.2 percent) with hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate.
absolute_effects.quote:
132 of those randomly assigned to enalapril (32.8 per-
cent) and 153 of those randomly assigned to hy-
dralazine-isosorbide dinitrate (38.2 percent)

absolute_effects.text: Sudden death, no warning: cumulative mortality 16% with enalapril vs 25% with hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate (P = 0.015).
Hospitalization for heart failure: 76 (18.9 percent) with enalapril vs 78 (18.4 percent) with hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate.
absolute_effects.quote:
76 of the patients as-
signed to enalapril (18.9 percent) and 78 of those as-
signed to hydralazine—isosorbide dinitrate (18.4 per-
cent) required hospitalization for the treatment of
heart failure.

harms.text: Headache was more frequent with hydralazine–isosorbide dinitrate; symptomatic hypotension and cough were more frequent with enalapril.

An excess of headache was noted in the
hydralazine—isosorbide dinitrate group, and an excess
of symptomatic hypotension and cough in the enala-
pril group.

harms.text: Laboratory values showed a higher incidence of azotemia in the enalapril group.

inclusion_criteria.text: Reduced exercise tolerance defined as dyspnea or fatigue at peak oxygen consumption <25 ml/kg/min.

ring at a peak oxygen consumption of less than 25 ml per kilogram

inclusion_criteria.text: Two consecutive exercise tests with respiratory stability and a stable clinical state were required before randomization.

gram per minute, with a difference between tests of <4 ml per
